question: Would you approve this as a future episode for this channel?

cards.viewer: Workers with a 401(k) match and high-interest credit card debt.
cards.decision: Should you pause 401(k) contributions beyond the match to pay cards faster?
cards.promise: We simulate the tradeoff using historical returns, payoff paths, and employer match rules.
cards.title: Invest or Kill Debt First?

cards.viewer: Single hourly workers earning $32 an hour full time who could add 8 extra hours of work a week.
cards.decision: Work those 8 hours as overtime at $48 an hour, or at a second job paying $48 an hour?
cards.promise: We run the full federal tax math on both paths, including the new overtime break, and find what a side job must pay to match.
cards.title: Overtime or a Second Job at $48 an Hour: Which Pays More?
cards.thumbObject: a time clock punch card beside a second work uniform

cards.viewer: People nearing retirement who can claim Social Security at 62, full retirement age, or 70.
cards.decision: Should you claim Social Security early or wait?
cards.promise: We compare lifetime spending paths under historical market returns and longevity assumptions.
cards.title: Claim Social Security Early?

cards.viewer: Married homeowners who bought their house in 2000 and are now weighing a sale to downsize.
cards.decision: Sell the house we bought in 2000 now, or keep it, given the $500,000 tax-free limit on home-sale gains?
cards.promise: We measure, metro by metro, how far typical home-price growth since 2000 has pushed sellers' gains against a limit that never moved with inflation.
cards.title: Bought Your Home in 2000? The $500,000 Tax-Free Limit Test
cards.thumbObject: a family house with a sold sign beside a capped glass jar

cards.viewer: Homeowners with a 7% mortgage quoted 6.5% and closing costs, unsure about refinancing.
cards.decision: Refinance the 7% mortgage to 6.5%, or keep the loan?
cards.promise: Using history, not a forecast, we'll model payments, closing costs, taxes, and moving patterns to test the refi choice.
cards.title: Should You Refinance Now?

cards.viewer: Workers whose paycheck withholding produces a federal tax refund of about $3,000 every spring.
cards.decision: Keep over-withholding for a $3,000 refund, or adjust withholding for bigger paychecks instead?
cards.promise: We price what parking that money with the government actually cost in interest, year by year, for savers and for card borrowers.
cards.title: Your $3,000 Tax Refund: What Is It Really Costing You?
cards.thumbObject: a tax refund check chained to a ticking kitchen timer

cards.viewer: New-car buyers in 2026 financing about $35,000 through a bank and torn between a 60-month and a 72-month loan.
cards.decision: Take the 72-month loan for the lower payment, or stick with 60 months?
cards.promise: Using years of real bank auto-loan rates, we measure how much the longer loan really adds and whether the rate or the time drives it.
cards.title: 60 vs 72 Months on a $35,000 Car Loan: The Real Cost
cards.thumbObject: Car key resting between loan contracts marked 60 and 72

cards.viewer: People in their 50s buying long-term care insurance they may not use for 20 years, choosing between a 3% and a 5% compound inflation option.
cards.decision: Is the 3% compound inflation option enough, or is the pricier 5% option worth paying for?
cards.promise: We run the 3% and 5% options through every 20-year stretch of nursing home prices on record to see how each kept pace.
cards.title: Long-Term Care Insurance: 3% or 5% Inflation Protection?
cards.thumbObject: Nursing home room with a daily price tag climbing stairs

cards.viewer: Savers in their 40s parking safe retirement money for 20 years, weighing savings bonds guaranteed to double against rolling T-bills.
cards.decision: Should I lock money in savings bonds that double in 20 years, or keep rolling T-bills instead?
cards.promise: We roll T-bills through every 20-year stretch since the Depression to see how often they managed to double your money.
cards.title: Savings Bonds That Double in 20 Years vs T-Bills
cards.thumbObject: Paper savings bond beside a stack of T-bills and a calendar

cards.viewer: Investors in the 24% tax bracket holding a $50,000 index fund position with a $10,000 gain, bought 11 months ago.
cards.decision: Sell now at the short-term tax rate, or wait a month for the lower long-term rate?
cards.promise: We replay every month-long stretch of recent market history to see how often waiting for the lower rate left investors with less after tax.
cards.title: Sell at 11 Months or Wait for the Lower Tax Rate?
cards.thumbObject: a desk calendar with its last page curling over a stock chart

cards.viewer: Home buyers in 2026 taking a 30-year mortgage at about 7%, whose lender offers one point to get 6.75%.
cards.decision: Pay one point to cut my rate from 7% to 6.75%, or skip it?
cards.promise: We replay the full weekly history of 30-year rates to see how often a refinance chance showed up before that point paid for itself.
cards.title: Paying a Point to Get 6.75%? What History Says
cards.thumbObject: Closing table with a calculator and a single gold coin

cards.viewer: Retirees keeping their next 5 years of spending in CDs or Treasuries at a time when 1-year rates top 5-year rates.
cards.decision: When a 1-year CD pays more than a 5-year CD, should I keep rolling the 1-year or lock the 5-year?
cards.promise: We replay every past stretch when 1-year yields topped 5-year yields and follow both choices to the end of the 5 years.
cards.title: 1-Year CD Pays More Than a 5-Year: Roll or Lock?
cards.thumbObject: Short and long CD certificates on a tilting balance scale

cards.viewer: Self-employed couples buying Marketplace health insurance and choosing Solo 401(k) contributions.
cards.decision: Should you make pre-tax Solo 401(k) contributions instead of Roth contributions?
cards.promise: We simulate taxes and health-credit changes to show which side of the tradeoff dominates.
cards.title: Solo 401(k): Roth or Pre-Tax?

cards.viewer: Homeowners who locked a 30-year mortgage at 3% in 2021 and have had about $500 a month to spare ever since.
cards.decision: Should my spare $500 a month go toward the 3% mortgage or into T-bills?
cards.promise: We replay every month since rates jumped to see which pile actually ended up bigger after federal income tax, and by how much.
cards.title: 3% Mortgage vs T-Bills: Where Should the $500 Have Gone?
cards.thumbObject: House key and a stack of T-bills on a balance scale

cards.viewer: Retirees around 65 buying an income annuity for 20 or more years of payments, choosing level checks or checks that rise 2% a year.
cards.decision: At 65, should I take the bigger level annuity check or the smaller check that rises 2% a year?
cards.promise: We test the 2% yearly raise against every 20-year stretch of US prices to see how its buying power actually held up.
cards.title: Does a 2% Annuity Raise Really Keep Up With Prices?
cards.thumbObject: Annuity check beside a grocery receipt with a small 2% arrow

cards.viewer: Parents with a child starting college and money in a 529 plan.
cards.decision: Should you spend 529 money before claiming a college tax credit?
cards.promise: We simulate qualified costs, credits, and account withdrawals to show how the ordering changes after-tax cash.
cards.title: 529 or Tax Credit?

cards.viewer: Grad students starting school in fall 2026 who need about $50,000 in private loans now that federal borrowing is capped.
cards.decision: Take a 7.5% variable rate or lock in 9% fixed for a 10-year payoff?
cards.promise: We run the variable loan through every 10-year stretch of short-term rate history to see how often the cheaper start ended up costing more.
cards.title: 7.5% Variable or 9% Fixed? Grad Loans Through History
cards.thumbObject: Graduation cap balanced on a seesaw between loan offers

cards.viewer: People carrying a $7,500 credit card balance at 24% who received a 0% transfer offer.
cards.decision: Take the 0% transfer with a 4% fee, or stay on the old card?
cards.promise: We'll simulate payoff calendars, fees, missed deadlines, and payment rules to test when the offer changes total cost.
cards.title: Is a Balance Transfer Worth It?
cards.thumbObject: credit cards beside a payoff calendar
